questions.q: How does the sqlite3 shell treat dot-commands such as .tables versus SQL statements?
options: Dot-commands need no semicolon; SQL statements end with a semicolon
Dot-commands need a semicolon; SQL does not
questions.explain: Dot-commands are shell-specific; SQL statements are ended by the semicolon.

questions.q: What is a SQLite database?
questions.explain: There is no server to install and no accounts or network needed.

questions.q: Which dot-command shows the CREATE TABLE statement for the students table?
questions.explain: .tables lists tables; .schema shows how a table was defined.

questions.q: What ends a SQL statement in the shell?
questions.explain: Statements can span multiple lines; indentation is only for human readability.

questions.q: Why list exact columns instead of SELECT * in application code?
options: It's explicit and doesn't break or change behavior if a column is added
questions.explain: SELECT * is fine for quick exploration in the shell.

questions.q: What does AS do in SELECT title AS book_title?
options: Renames the column in the table
Gives the column an alias in the result
questions.explain: AS is optional but improves readability, and aliases are essential for expressions.

questions.q: Which query computes a 10% discounted price column?
options: SELECT title, price * 0.9 AS discounted_price FROM books;
questions.explain: You can compute values in SELECT, not just read stored columns.

questions.q: What does the lesson say SELECT retrieves?
options: Data, and most of SQL revolves around shaping a SELECT
questions.explain: Getting comfortable with SELECT's anatomy pays off for the rest of the course.

questions.q: Which operator has higher precedence, AND or OR?
questions.explain: Use parentheses whenever you mix them, since relying on precedence is a common source of bugs.

questions.q: Is BETWEEN 1960 AND 1990 inclusive?
questions.explain: It equals >= 1960 AND <= 1990.

questions.q: Which clause matches a column against a set of values?
questions.explain: IN is a shorthand for several OR comparisons on the same column.

questions.q: When is WHERE evaluated?
options: Per row, before any grouping or sorting
questions.explain: WHERE narrows the result set down to rows that match.

questions.q: Without ORDER BY, what does SQL guarantee about row order?
options: Nothing; the order can vary between runs
questions.explain: The database may return rows in whatever order is convenient internally.

questions.q: What does ORDER BY genre ASC, price DESC do?
options: Sorts genres A–Z, and within each genre sorts price highest to lowest
questions.explain: Ties in the first column are broken by the next, each with its own direction.

questions.q: Why avoid ORDER BY 2 in real code?
options: Adding or reordering selected columns silently changes what it sorts by
questions.explain: Sort by column name instead.

questions.q: Where does SQLite place NULLs in ascending order?
questions.explain: Other databases differ: Postgres defaults to NULLS LAST for ASC.

questions.q: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(genre)?
options: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(genre) counts only rows where genre is not NULL
questions.explain: COUNT(column) ignores NULLs in that column.

questions.q: What rule applies to non-aggregated columns in a SELECT with GROUP BY?
options: Each must appear in the GROUP BY
questions.explain: SELECT genre, title, AVG(price) ... GROUP BY genre is invalid because SQL wouldn't know which title to show.

questions.q: What does GROUP BY genre with COUNT(*) return?
options: One row per genre with the number of books in it
questions.explain: It splits rows into buckets by value and computes the aggregate for each.

questions.q: Which function returns the highest price?
questions.explain: The five core aggregates are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX.

questions.q: Why is The Lathe of Heaven missing from the INNER JOIN result?
options: INNER JOIN drops the last row
Its author_id is NULL, so it has no match in authors
questions.explain: INNER JOIN returns only rows where both sides match.

questions.q: What does LEFT JOIN do with a left row that has no match?
options: Keeps it and fills the right table's columns with NULL
questions.explain: It keeps every row from the left table.

questions.q: How do you find only books with no known author after a LEFT JOIN?
questions.explain: Filtering for NULL on the right table's key exposes the unmatched rows.

questions.q: When are table aliases required?
options: When two tables share a column name such as id, and they keep long queries readable
questions.explain: For example, books AS b and authors AS a.

questions.q: What does SELECT * FROM books WHERE price = NULL return?
questions.explain: Comparing unknown to anything yields unknown, which SQL treats as not true.

questions.q: What is the correct way to find rows with no price?
questions.explain: Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.

questions.q: What does COALESCE(discontinued_reason, 'still in print') return for a NULL reason?
questions.explain: COALESCE returns the first argument that isn't NULL.

questions.q: What does price + 1 give when price is NULL?
questions.explain: NULL propagates through arithmetic instead of being treated as zero.

questions.q: What does CREATE TABLE produce?
options: An empty table: the structure with no rows
questions.explain: It defines columns, types and rules.

questions.q: What happens on INSERT INTO books (price) VALUES (9.99) when title is NOT NULL?
options: It inserts with an empty title
It fails with a NOT NULL constraint error
questions.explain: Error: NOT NULL constraint failed: books.title.

questions.q: What is special about INTEGER PRIMARY KEY in SQLite?
options: It auto-increments and aliases the internal row ID
It is stored as a blob
questions.explain: AUTOINCREMENT is only for edge cases where IDs must never be reused.

questions.q: What does a DEFAULT value allow?
options: Omitting the column from INSERT so SQLite fills it in
questions.explain: For example in_stock INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1.

questions.q: What happens if you run UPDATE books SET price = 0 with no WHERE clause?
questions.explain: Verify with an equivalent SELECT ... WHERE first.

questions.q: Why list column names explicitly in INSERT?
options: It is self-documenting and doesn't break if column order changes
questions.explain: INSERT INTO books (title, author, price) is preferred over relying on column order.

questions.q: What does DELETE FROM books; do?
options: Removes every row, but the table itself still exists
questions.explain: The table remains, now empty.

questions.q: What does INSERT OR REPLACE do when the primary key already exists?
questions.explain: In the settings example, theme becomes 'light'.

questions.q: Why does query 2 use LEFT JOIN?
options: Books with no known author still appear
questions.explain: 'Unknown Author Book' has a NULL author_id.

questions.q: What does HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 do in query 4?
options: Keeps only authors with two or more books
questions.explain: HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

questions.q: Which tables make up the project database?
questions.explain: It's a two-table library database.

questions.q: What does in_stock INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 mean?
options: The column is optional with no default
Every book must have a value, and it defaults to 1 (in stock)
questions.explain: The seed data uses 0 for out-of-stock books.

questions.q: Why does the employee/manager self-join use LEFT JOIN?
options: INNER JOIN is invalid for self-joins
Alice has no manager, and INNER JOIN would drop her
questions.explain: manager_id IS NULL for Alice.

questions.q: What does a self-join require?
options: Two distinct aliases for the same table
questions.explain: Without aliases SQL can't tell which copy a column belongs to.

questions.q: Why is WHERE d.active = 1 wrong in the LEFT JOIN example?
options: It filters out unmatched rows, turning the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN
questions.explain: Alice, Carol and Frank vanished; put the active check in ON instead.

questions.q: What is the single most common LEFT JOIN bug per the lesson?
questions.explain: Conditions on the right table belong in ON to preserve unmatched left rows.

questions.q: What is a scalar subquery?
options: One that returns exactly one row and one column
questions.explain: If it returns more than one row, SQLite raises an error.

questions.q: What does WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) return?
options: Customers who have at least one order
questions.explain: Dave has never ordered, so he's excluded.

questions.q: What makes a subquery correlated?
options: It references a column from the outer query, so it runs for each outer row
questions.explain: It can't be evaluated once up front.

questions.q: In the AVG example, how many times does the inner query run?
options: Once; the outer query compares every amount to that single value
questions.explain: It's uncorrelated, so it computes the average once.

questions.q: How do set operations combine results compared with joins?
options: Vertically, stacking rows of two SELECTs; joins combine horizontally
questions.explain: Set operations are the SQL equivalent of union, intersection and difference.

questions.q: What is the rule for SELECTs combined with a set operator?
options: They must use the same table
They must return the same number of columns with compatible types
questions.explain: The result uses the first query's column names; mismatched counts fail with a parse error.

questions.q: How do UNION and UNION ALL differ?
options: UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps every row
questions.explain: UNION ALL gives accurate row counts and is faster on large sets.

questions.q: Where must ORDER BY go in a UNION query?
options: After the last SELECT, applying to the combined result
questions.explain: It is not attached to an individual query.

questions.q: Why does LENGTH('  Alice Nguyen  ') return 16 while the name looks like 12 characters?
questions.explain: TRIM brings it back to 12.

questions.q: What does SUBSTR(string, start, length) do, and how is it indexed?
questions.explain: Combined with INSTR you can pull out a first name.

questions.q: Why normalize case with LOWER() before comparing user-entered text?
options: 'Alice' and 'alice' are different strings for = in most databases
questions.explain: SQLite comparison is case-sensitive by default.

questions.q: Which function strips leading and trailing whitespace?
questions.explain: LTRIM and RTRIM do one side only.

questions.q: How is a searched CASE evaluated?
options: Top to bottom, stopping at the first matching WHEN
questions.explain: Order matters; put the narrowest condition first.

questions.q: What does CASE return when no WHEN matches and there is no ELSE?
questions.explain: Order 3 with status_code 3 shows NULL in the example.

questions.q: When is the simple CASE form useful?
options: When every branch compares the same expression against specific values
questions.explain: CASE status_code WHEN 1 THEN ... is equivalent to repeated equality tests.

questions.q: Where can CASE be used?
options: In SELECT, WHERE or ORDER BY
questions.explain: It is SQL's inline if/else.

questions.q: What is a view?
options: A SELECT query saved under a name, queryable like a table
A copy of the table's data
questions.explain: It doesn't store data itself.

questions.q: When does a view's underlying query run?
options: Every time you query the view
questions.explain: It runs fresh against the real tables.

questions.q: What is a key benefit of the category_revenue view?
options: The join and GROUP BY logic is defined once and can be fixed in one place
questions.explain: Views hide complexity.

questions.q: Why is Mechanical Keyboard missing from in_stock_products?
options: Its stock is 0 and the view filters WHERE stock > 0
questions.explain: The WHERE filter is applied automatically every time.

questions.q: What does a SCAN in EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN mean?
options: SQLite checked every row in the table
questions.explain: On 5 million rows that would be very slow; SEARCH ... USING INDEX jumps almost directly to the match.

questions.q: What is an index, per the lesson?
options: A separate sorted structure that lets the database find rows without checking every row
questions.explain: It is like a book's index.

questions.q: Does the idx_<table>_<column> naming pattern affect how an index works?
options: No, it's just a common readable habit
questions.explain: Any valid name works.

questions.q: What does the order of columns in a composite index determine?
options: What the index is useful for
questions.explain: The country, signup_date index suits filtering by country first, then signup_date.

questions.q: What is the SQLite surprise about foreign keys?
options: They're parsed but not enforced unless you turn enforcement on
questions.explain: The Ghost Book with author_id 999 was inserted without error.

questions.q: How do you enable foreign key enforcement?
options: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; on every connection
questions.explain: The setting isn't persisted in the database file.

questions.q: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?
options: Deletes child rows automatically when the parent row is deleted
questions.explain: Deleting Asimov removed both of his books.

questions.q: What do constraints do in general?
options: Reject bad data at insert or update time
questions.explain: They stop bad data causing bugs later.

questions.q: What does a transaction provide?
options: An all-or-nothing unit of work across several statements
questions.explain: It prevents inconsistent states such as money debited but never credited.

questions.q: What does ROLLBACK do?
questions.explain: It is as if the transaction never happened.

questions.q: In SQLite's default mode, what happens when a statement fails mid-transaction due to a constraint?
options: Only that statement is aborted; the transaction stays open with earlier changes pending
The whole transaction is rolled back automatically
questions.explain: You must issue ROLLBACK (or handle it) yourself.

questions.q: What happens outside an explicit BEGIN?
options: Each statement runs in its own implicit one-statement transaction
questions.explain: This is insufficient for multi-step changes like a transfer.

questions.q: Why does the schema have an order_items table?
options: One order has many products and a product appears in many orders: a many-to-many relationship via a junction table
questions.explain: It uses a composite PRIMARY KEY of (order_id, product_id).

questions.q: Why is unit_price stored on order_items instead of looked up from products?
options: Historical orders stay accurate if a product's price later changes
questions.explain: The price at the time of sale is preserved.

questions.q: Which four tables does the project use?
questions.explain: The schema is realistic enough to need joins, subqueries, views, CASE and transactions.

questions.q: What does CHECK (price > 0) enforce?
questions.explain: Constraints reject bad data at insert or update time.

questions.q: How does a window function differ from GROUP BY?
options: Each input row keeps its own line while gaining a computed column
It collapses rows into one per group
It only works on one table
questions.explain: Window functions handle top-N per group, running totals and period comparisons that GROUP BY cannot express.

questions.q: What does PARTITION BY region do?
options: Splits rows into independent windows, one per region, each restarting numbering
questions.explain: ORDER BY inside OVER decides the order within each partition.

questions.q: For Bob's two tied 800.0 rows in West, what do RANK and DENSE_RANK show?
questions.explain: ROW_NUMBER still gives 4 and 5, since it always assigns unique sequential numbers.

questions.q: What syntax marks a function as a window function?
questions.explain: Every window function is a normal function followed by OVER (...).

questions.q: What is a CTE?
options: A named temporary result set defined with WITH and used like a table in that query
questions.explain: CTEs make complex queries readable, naming each step instead of nesting subqueries.

questions.q: What can a recursive CTE do that a normal one cannot?
options: Reference itself, walking hierarchies of unknown depth
questions.explain: It is the standard SQL way to walk org charts, category trees and folders.

questions.q: What does the self-referencing manager_id make the employees data?
questions.explain: It points to another row in the same table.

questions.q: Can CTEs reference each other in one query?
options: No, only one CTE is allowed
Yes, chained with commas, each with its own name
questions.explain: This avoids another indentation level for each step.

questions.q: What does EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN do?
options: Shows the plan SQLite would use without running the query
questions.explain: It tells you whether SQLite scans many rows or uses an index.

questions.q: What is the single most common optimization per the lesson?
options: Index the columns your WHERE clauses filter on
questions.explain: It changes SCAN into SEARCH ... USING INDEX.

questions.q: What does SEARCH ... USING INDEX mean?
options: A B-tree lookup instead of a full scan
questions.explain: SQLite jumps directly to the matching rows.

questions.q: In the join example, why did SQLite make customers the outer loop?
options: It has only 5 rows, so it scans them and searches orders by index for each match
questions.explain: Plan order matters in joins.

questions.q: Does SQLite have stored procedures?
options: No, there is no CREATE PROCEDURE
questions.explain: The lesson refuses to show syntax that doesn't run.

questions.q: What does SQLite offer instead, per the lesson?
options: Transactions driven from application code and user-defined functions
questions.explain: The transfer_funds example does this in Python.

questions.q: Why does the 'reduce round-trips' reason mostly not apply to SQLite?
options: It is embedded and in-process, with no separate server
It has no network at all
questions.explain: There's no server to send a CALL to.

questions.q: What does the transfer_funds example guarantee?
options: The debit and credit run as one atomic SQL transaction
questions.explain: It checks the balance, updates both accounts, and commits (rolling back on failure).

questions.q: Inside a trigger body, what do OLD and NEW refer to?
options: The row before the change and the row after it
questions.explain: In the audit trigger, OLD.stock is 50 and NEW.stock is 45.

questions.q: What does AFTER UPDATE OF stock mean?
options: The trigger fires only when the stock column changes, after the change is made
questions.explain: Updating name alone wouldn't fire it.

questions.q: How does the BEFORE trigger block a bad write?
options: SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'message') when the WHEN condition is true
questions.explain: BEFORE runs before the row is written, so it can veto the change.

questions.q: Does SQLite support triggers?
options: Yes, fully, with real CREATE TRIGGER syntax
questions.explain: Unlike stored procedures, triggers are natively supported.

questions.q: What is the update anomaly?
options: One real-world fact needing multiple easy-to-miss writes, leaving inconsistent copies
questions.explain: Nadia ended up with two different emails depending on the row.

questions.q: What does 1NF require?
options: Each column holds a single atomic value
Every non-key column depends on the whole key
questions.explain: No comma-separated lists crammed into one field.

questions.q: What is normalization's goal per the lesson?
options: Store each fact in exactly one place
questions.explain: The payoff is that updates, inserts and deletes can't silently corrupt data.

questions.q: What does 3NF require of non-key columns?
options: They depend on the key and nothing but the key
They depend on part of a composite key
questions.explain: 2NF requires dependence on the whole primary key.

questions.q: How does SQLite store JSON?
options: As plain TEXT, parsed on demand by JSON functions
In a dedicated JSON column type
questions.explain: SQLite has no dedicated JSON column type.

questions.q: What does the ->> operator return compared with ->?
options: ->> unquotes the result into plain SQL text; -> keeps it as JSON
questions.explain: -> is useful when passing the result into another JSON function.

questions.q: How can you guarantee well-formed JSON at write time?
options: Use json_valid() in a CHECK constraint
questions.explain: SQLite stores text with no schema enforcement otherwise.

questions.q: What does json_each do?
options: Turns a JSON array into one row per element
questions.explain: It's a table-valued function, used with a comma join per source row.

questions.q: Why is LIKE '%database%' a poor choice for text search?
options: It can't rank by relevance and a leading % forces a full scan
questions.explain: FTS5 provides word indexing, ranking, phrase and prefix queries.

questions.q: How do you create a full-text searchable table?
questions.explain: It looks like a normal table but is backed by an inverted index.

questions.q: How do you query an FTS5 table for a word?
questions.explain: MATCH performs a real word-index lookup.

questions.q: In FTS5's rank column, which values are more relevant?
questions.explain: ORDER BY rank without DESC gives best-match-first (BM25).

questions.q: Why does ADD COLUMN with NOT NULL require a DEFAULT in SQLite?
options: SQLite must backfill existing rows with something
NOT NULL is not allowed otherwise
questions.explain: Existing rows immediately get the default (e.g. 'active').

questions.q: What must you do when renaming a column with RENAME COLUMN?
options: Update application code that references the old name at the same time
questions.explain: Reads and writes against the old column name fail once the migration runs.

questions.q: Which change still needs the table-rebuild pattern?
options: Adding a column with a default
Adding a CHECK constraint to an existing table
Dropping a column on recent SQLite
questions.explain: ALTER TABLE can't add a CHECK, change a column type, or add UNIQUE/FOREIGN KEY to an existing table.

questions.q: What is the rebuild pattern's outline?
options: Create a new table in the desired shape, copy the data across, then swap names
questions.explain: The lesson runs it inside a transaction with foreign keys temporarily off.

questions.q: Why does the project index every foreign key column?
options: Every one of them gets joined on
questions.explain: Examples: idx_orders_customer_id and idx_order_items_product_id.

questions.q: What is order_items' role in the schema?
options: Junction table for the many-to-many between orders and products, carrying quantity
questions.explain: quantity is data specific to that pairing.

questions.q: Why does the schema have a separate categories table?
options: Normalization: each category fact is stored once
questions.explain: products reference it with category_id.

questions.q: What does categories.name UNIQUE enforce?
options: No two categories share a name
questions.explain: It is a constraint on the data.

questions.q: Can an index on (dept, last_name) speed up a query filtering only on last_name?
options: No, it falls back to a SCAN (leftmost-prefix rule)
questions.explain: A B-tree is sorted by its first column first, like a phone book sorted by city then name.

questions.q: What is a covering index?
options: An index containing all the columns the query needs, so the table is never opened
questions.explain: SELECT dept, salary with an index on (dept, salary) shows USING COVERING INDEX.

questions.q: What breaks a covering index?
options: Selecting a column not in the index, e.g. SELECT *
questions.explain: The plan reverts to a normal SEARCH that also visits the table row.

questions.q: Which column should come first in a composite index?
options: The one your queries filter on most consistently
questions.explain: That is the leftmost-prefix rule.

questions.q: Why was one transaction about 239x faster than 2000 separate commits?
options: Each COMMIT forces a durable disk flush, and one transaction does it once
questions.explain: Batching related writes is the single highest-leverage performance fix.

questions.q: What does WAL mode change for concurrency?
options: Readers can keep reading the last-committed state while a write happens
questions.explain: The default delete journal mode locks the database file during a write, blocking readers.

questions.q: Does PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL matter for an in-memory database?
options: No, there is no file to journal
questions.explain: It matters for file-backed databases under concurrent load.

questions.q: What does cache_size control?
options: How many pages SQLite keeps cached in memory
questions.explain: A negative value is interpreted as an amount of memory rather than a page count.

questions.q: Does SQLite have built-in partitioning?
options: No; the manual pattern is separate tables presented via a view
questions.explain: Postgres and MySQL have native support; SQLite does not.

questions.q: Why is dropping a partition better than DELETE ... WHERE for old data?
options: It avoids finding and removing matching rows one at a time
questions.explain: Retention becomes a drop-the-partition operation.

questions.q: What is partition pruning?
options: The planner skipping partitions irrelevant to the query
questions.explain: A query for this month's orders only touches this month's partition.

questions.q: In the manual SQLite pattern, how does application code see the data?
options: As one events view built with UNION ALL over the separate tables
questions.explain: The view hides that two tables back it, but you manage routing yourself.

questions.q: What is the difference between replication and backup?
options: Replication keeps live copies in sync for availability and read scaling; backup is a restorable snapshot against data loss
questions.explain: SQLite has no replication but supports backup well.

questions.q: What does .backup produce?
options: A consistent point-in-time copy of the database file, safe while it's in use
questions.explain: Rows inserted afterward do not appear in backup.db.

questions.q: How does .dump differ from .backup?
options: It produces portable, readable SQL, but restores slower for large databases
questions.explain: Restore with sqlite3 new.db < dump.sql.

questions.q: Which statement fits the checklist?
options: Keep backups on the same disk
questions.explain: An untested backup is an assumption, not a guarantee.

questions.q: How did the attacker log in as admin with the input admin'--?
options: The quote closed the string and -- commented out the password check
questions.explain: The database never evaluated the AND password = ... part.

questions.q: What is the fix demonstrated?
questions.explain: The same malicious input returns an empty result.

questions.q: Why does string concatenation make injection possible?
options: Input becomes literal SQL text instead of a value
questions.explain: Anything a caller passes becomes part of the query itself.

questions.q: Which are other injection shapes the lesson mentions?
questions.explain: One matches every row; the other runs a second destructive statement.

questions.q: Which describes NoSQL accurately?
options: An umbrella for document, key-value, wide-column and graph databases
questions.explain: Each trades away parts of the relational model for something else.

questions.q: How do relationships typically differ between SQL and document stores?
options: SQL uses JOINs across normalized tables; document stores usually embed related data (denormalized)
questions.explain: From the lesson's comparison table.

questions.q: What does Priya's extra preferences object show in the JSON example?
options: Per-row fields without a schema migration
questions.explain: It's the flexibility of a document store, achieved via a JSON TEXT column.

questions.q: Which is generally easier to scale horizontally?
options: Many NoSQL systems, designed to scale out from day one
questions.explain: Relational systems traditionally scale up on a bigger server.

questions.q: What does setting conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row allow?
options: Accessing columns by name (and dict(row) for JSON-ready output)
questions.explain: By default sqlite3 returns plain tuples, which get unreadable fast.

questions.q: How should values be passed into SQL from application code?
questions.explain: It's the same parameterization from the security module.

questions.q: What does executemany do?
options: Runs one INSERT per tuple in a list, the idiomatic way to batch inserts
questions.explain: Still wrap it in a single transaction rather than committing after each.

questions.q: Why does the lesson use Python's sqlite3 as the example?
options: Its patterns map onto other languages' drivers (psycopg2, JDBC, mysql2)
questions.explain: Parameterized queries, connections/cursors and transaction handling are common patterns.

questions.q: What is OLTP optimized for compared to OLAP?
options: Fast, small, frequent reads/writes; OLAP is for large scans over history
Large scans; OLAP is for small writes
questions.explain: OLTP: 'record this order'; OLAP: 'total revenue by region, last 8 quarters'.

questions.q: What is the fact table in a star schema?
options: One row per measurable event, holding numeric measures and foreign keys to dimensions
questions.explain: fact_sales holds quantity and revenue with keys to dim_customer, dim_product and dim_date.

questions.q: What does a dimension table describe?
options: One axis you'd want to slice by, such as customer, product or date
questions.explain: They surround the fact table, like the points of a star.

questions.q: How does schema shape differ between OLTP and OLAP?
options: OLTP is normalized for fast writes; OLAP is denormalized (star) for scanning and aggregation
questions.explain: Data freshness also differs: warehouses often load in batches.

questions.q: Why use an in-memory SQLite database rather than a mock to test database code?
options: It's a real database that enforces constraints and transactions, so tests catch real violations
questions.explain: A mock only tests that you call the right methods.

questions.q: What does an in-memory database do when the connection closes?
options: It disappears, giving isolation between test runs
questions.explain: It's fast (no disk I/O) and isolated.

questions.q: What does transfer() do when funds are insufficient?
questions.explain: The except block calls conn.rollback() and re-raises.

questions.q: Why does the test's setUp create the schema and seed rows each time?
options: Each test starts from a known clean state
questions.explain: It uses sqlite3.connect(":memory:") with executescript.

questions.q: Why does unit_price on order_items deliberately duplicate products.price?
options: products.price can change later, but an order must keep the price the customer paid
questions.explain: The lesson calls this the correct call, not an oversight.

questions.q: What does the CHECK on orders.status enforce?
options: Only pending, paid, shipped or cancelled are allowed
questions.explain: It is a constraint with an IN list.

questions.q: What is order_audit maintained by?
questions.explain: The capstone includes a trigger that maintains an audit trail.

questions.q: Which pieces does the capstone combine?
options: Normalized schema, indexes, trigger, full-text search, JSON metadata and a verified query plan
questions.explain: It is a complete small order-management database run end to end.

questions.q:
Use this data for the next questions: books(id, title, genre, price, author_id) holds Dune/Sci-Fi/9.99/1, Foundation/Sci-Fi/8.5/2, Snow Crash/Cyber/10.5/NULL, Hobbit/Fantasy/6.99/3, Neuromancer/Cyber/7.25/NULL; authors holds 1 Herbert, 2 Asimov, 3 Tolkien.
What does `SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(author_id) FROM books;` return?
questions.explain: COUNT(*) counts all 5 rows; COUNT(author_id) skips the two NULLs.

questions.q:
Use this data for the next questions: books(id, title, genre, price, author_id) holds Dune/Sci-Fi/9.99/1, Foundation/Sci-Fi/8.5/2, Snow Crash/Cyber/10.5/NULL, Hobbit/Fantasy/6.99/3, Neuromancer/Cyber/7.25/NULL; authors holds 1 Herbert, 2 Asimov, 3 Tolkien.
What does `SELECT genre, COUNT(*) FROM books GROUP BY genre HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY genre;` return?
questions.explain: HAVING filters groups after aggregation, dropping Fantasy (1 book).

questions.q:
Use this data for the next questions: books(id, title, genre, price, author_id) holds Dune/Sci-Fi/9.99/1, Foundation/Sci-Fi/8.5/2, Snow Crash/Cyber/10.5/NULL, Hobbit/Fantasy/6.99/3, Neuromancer/Cyber/7.25/NULL; authors holds 1 Herbert, 2 Asimov, 3 Tolkien.
Which books come back from a LEFT JOIN of books to authors filtered with `WHERE a.id IS NULL`?
questions.explain: The two books with a NULL author_id have no matching author row.

questions.q:
Use this data for the next questions: books(id, title, genre, price, author_id) holds Dune/Sci-Fi/9.99/1, Foundation/Sci-Fi/8.5/2, Snow Crash/Cyber/10.5/NULL, Hobbit/Fantasy/6.99/3, Neuromancer/Cyber/7.25/NULL; authors holds 1 Herbert, 2 Asimov, 3 Tolkien.
How many rows does `SELECT * FROM books WHERE author_id = NULL;` return?
questions.explain: Comparing to NULL with = is never true; you need IS NULL.

questions.q:
Use this data for the next questions: books(id, title, genre, price, author_id) holds Dune/Sci-Fi/9.99/1, Foundation/Sci-Fi/8.5/2, Snow Crash/Cyber/10.5/NULL, Hobbit/Fantasy/6.99/3, Neuromancer/Cyber/7.25/NULL; authors holds 1 Herbert, 2 Asimov, 3 Tolkien.
What does `SELECT title FROM books WHERE price BETWEEN 7 AND 9 ORDER BY title;` return?
questions.explain: BETWEEN is inclusive: 8.5 and 7.25 qualify; 9.99 and 6.99 do not.

questions.q:
Use this data for the next questions: books(id, title, genre, price, author_id) holds Dune/Sci-Fi/9.99/1, Foundation/Sci-Fi/8.5/2, Snow Crash/Cyber/10.5/NULL, Hobbit/Fantasy/6.99/3, Neuromancer/Cyber/7.25/NULL; authors holds 1 Herbert, 2 Asimov, 3 Tolkien.
What does `SELECT title FROM books ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 2;` return?
questions.explain: Sorted by price descending, the top two are 10.5 and 9.99.

questions.q:
Use this data for the next questions: books(id, title, genre, price, author_id) holds Dune/Sci-Fi/9.99/1, Foundation/Sci-Fi/8.5/2, Snow Crash/Cyber/10.5/NULL, Hobbit/Fantasy/6.99/3, Neuromancer/Cyber/7.25/NULL; authors holds 1 Herbert, 2 Asimov, 3 Tolkien.
In `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY genre ORDER BY price DESC)`, what rank does Neuromancer get?
questions.explain: Within Cyber, Snow Crash (10.5) ranks 1 and Neuromancer (7.25) ranks 2.

questions.q:
Use this data for the next questions: books(id, title, genre, price, author_id) holds Dune/Sci-Fi/9.99/1, Foundation/Sci-Fi/8.5/2, Snow Crash/Cyber/10.5/NULL, Hobbit/Fantasy/6.99/3, Neuromancer/Cyber/7.25/NULL; authors holds 1 Herbert, 2 Asimov, 3 Tolkien.
What does `SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN price > 8 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM books;` return?
questions.explain: Dune, Foundation and Snow Crash are above 8.

questions.q: A report must list every customer, including those with no orders. Which join do you use?
options: LEFT JOIN from customers to orders
questions.explain: LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched left rows, filling NULLs for the right side.

questions.q: Your LEFT JOIN with `WHERE d.active = 1` silently drops employees whose department is inactive or missing. What is the fix?
options: Move the condition into the ON clause
questions.explain: A WHERE on the right table turns the join into an inner join; put the filter in ON.

questions.q: A bank transfer must debit one account and credit another, or do neither. What do you use?
questions.explain: A transaction makes the two updates atomic; ROLLBACK undoes both on failure.

questions.q: In SQLite, a book row references author 999, which doesn't exist, and no error appears. What did you forget?
questions.explain: SQLite parses foreign keys but only enforces them when the pragma is on for the connection.

questions.q: A query filtering `WHERE email = ?` on a 5-million-row table runs a full SCAN. What is the most direct fix?
questions.explain: An index turns the SCAN into a SEARCH ... USING INDEX.

questions.q: You have an index on (dept, last_name). Which query can NOT use it effectively?
questions.explain: The leftmost-prefix rule: filtering only on the second column can't use the index.

questions.q: Login code builds `SELECT ... WHERE username = '` + input + `'`. A user types `admin'--`. What happens?
options: The quote closes the string and -- comments out the rest, bypassing the password check
questions.explain: This is SQL injection; parameterized queries pass the input as data instead.

questions.q: 2,000 INSERTs run much faster when wrapped in one transaction instead of committing each. Why?
options: Each COMMIT forces a durable disk flush, so one transaction flushes once
questions.explain: Batching writes is the highest-leverage performance fix.

questions.q: A table stores customer name, email and product price on every order row, and an email change leaves two versions. Which problem is this and what is the cure?
options: An update anomaly; normalize so each fact is stored once
A trigger bug; drop the trigger
questions.explain: Normalization stores each fact in one place, so one update stays consistent.

questions.q: When should you choose a view?
options: To store a copy of the data
To save a complex join/aggregate under a name so everyone reuses one definition
questions.explain: A view stores the query, not the data; it runs fresh each time.

questions.q: What does a trigger `AFTER UPDATE OF stock ON products` let you do?
options: Automatically write an audit row recording OLD and NEW stock
questions.explain: Triggers run automatically on data changes, with OLD and NEW row references.

questions.q: You need to run dashboards over years of order history without slowing the live ordering system. Which design fits?
options: A separate OLAP star schema (fact and dimension tables) loaded in batches
questions.explain: OLTP is for fast small writes; OLAP star schemas are for large scans and aggregation.

challenges.title: Top spender per genre
challenges.prompt: Given a `books` table (title, genre, price), write a query that returns each genre with its highest price, ordered by genre. Use the sample data from the questions above.
challenges.solution: SELECT genre, MAX(price) FROM books GROUP BY genre ORDER BY genre;
challenges.explain: GROUP BY genre makes one group per genre and MAX(price) takes the highest price in each.

challenges.title: Books with no author
challenges.prompt: Using `books` and `authors` (id, name), list the titles of books that have no matching author, ordered by title, using a LEFT JOIN.
challenges.solution: SELECT b.title FROM books b LEFT JOIN authors a ON a.id = b.author_id WHERE a.id IS NULL ORDER BY b.title;
challenges.explain: LEFT JOIN keeps every book; the unmatched ones have a NULL author id, which you test with IS NULL.
